label: Causation
definition_short: The principle by which higher realities bring lower realities into being through eternal emanation; creative causation that is neither efficient production nor material composition but the overflow of being and goodness.
definition_long:
Causation in Neoplatonic philosophy denotes the metaphysical principle by which higher realities give rise to lower realities in a continuous, eternal overflow. This Neoplatonic understanding of causation differs fundamentally from both Aristotelian efficient causation, in which a cause acts upon matter to produce an effect, and from material causation, in which causes are temporally prior to effects. In Neoplatonism, causation is understood through the doctrine of emanation: the One, as the infinite source of all being and goodness, eternally overflows, producing the Divine Intellect; the Divine Intellect, in its eternal contemplation of the One, eternally overflows, producing the World Soul; the World Soul, in its eternal activity, eternally produces and sustains the sensible cosmos. This causal process is not a temporal sequence but an eternal and simultaneous relationship of dependence and expression.

The Neoplatonic doctrine of causation solves a profound metaphysical problem: how can the infinite and eternal One, which is absolutely simple and unchanging, give rise to a multiplicity of finite, complex, and changing beings without undergoing change itself or becoming less than it is? The answer lies in understanding causation as emanation. The One does not consciously create the universe as an external artisan might craft a work. Rather, the One's absolute fullness and fecundity necessarily overflow, just as the sun radiates light without becoming less luminous, just as a fire emanates heat without being diminished. This overflow is not an external act but the natural expression of the One's infinite nature. The One remains eternally what it is—the absolute source, beyond being and non-being, beyond all determinate categories—while eternally giving rise to all that exists.

In Plotinus's account, the Divine Intellect, as the immediate product of the One's overflow, eternally contemplates the One and through this eternal contemplative activity constitutes the realm of intelligible forms. The Divine Intellect is not separate from the One, nor does it exhaust the One; rather, it exists in eternal, intimate relationship with its source. The multiplicity of intelligible forms that characterize the Divine Intellect are not separate entities but rather the multiple expressions of the One's infinite perfection perceived from the perspective of multiplicity. The Divine Intellect simultaneously knows itself, knows all intelligible forms in their eternal distinctness, and knows the One from which it eternally derives. This triple knowing constitutes the dynamic life of the Divine Intellect.

The World Soul, in turn, proceeds from the Divine Intellect. Like the Divine Intellect in relation to the One, the World Soul eternally contemplates the Divine Intellect and through this contemplation constitutes the ordering principle of the sensible cosmos. The World Soul does not create the material world through deliberate decision or conscious effort; rather, its eternal life and activity necessarily give rise to and sustain the sensible order. The World Soul maintains the cosmic order through its eternal contemplation of the intelligible forms, transmitting their eternal patterns into the realm of temporal becoming. The sensible cosmos, with its orderly motion of the celestial spheres, the cycling of seasons, the generation and corruption of sublunary things, all flow from and depend upon the World Soul's eternal organizing activity.

Individual souls proceed from the World Soul in a similar manner. Each human soul, while also capable of choosing to identify with particular embodied consciousness, is eternally connected to and dependent upon the World Soul. This eternal connection is not broken by incarnation; even while the soul is embodied and appears separate, it remains eternally rooted in and dependent upon the World Soul's life. This explains how individual souls can retain knowledge of intelligible realities and can undertake the ascent back toward their source: they have never truly separated from their source; they remain eternally participants in the cosmic intelligence of the World Soul and the Divine Intellect.

The Neoplatonic understanding of causation incorporates several crucial distinctions. First, it distinguishes clearly between the cause and the effect: the One is not identical to the Divine Intellect, the Divine Intellect is not identical to the World Soul, the World Soul is not identical to the sensible cosmos. Each level maintains its own nature and ontological status. Yet simultaneously, there is an intimate continuity and dependency: the lower depends absolutely on the higher for its being, character, and activity. Second, it distinguishes between causation and generation or production: the One does not generate the Divine Intellect in the sense of making something that was not; rather, the Divine Intellect eternally exists as a direct expression of the One's nature. Third, it emphasizes that causation is simultaneous and eternal: there is no temporal priority of cause to effect, but rather an eternal relationship of dependence in which the cause eternally sustains the effect in being.

The doctrine of causation connects intimately with the concept of participation. All reality below the One is caused by and dependent upon what is above it; this dependence is precisely what constitutes participation. To participate is to be caused by, to depend upon, to be an expression of a higher reality. The sensible world participates in the intelligible world; individual souls participate in the World Soul; all beings participate in the Divine Intellect; all reality participates in the One. Through this cascade of participation, the infinite goodness and being of the One manifests throughout the entire cosmos, making all things genuinely real and good insofar as they participate in their source.

Plotinus emphasizes that the relationship between cause and effect is intrinsic to the nature of each. The One is eternally generative not because of any external pressure or internal need but because this is its very nature. The Divine Intellect is eternally contemplative of and dependent upon the One because this is what the Divine Intellect is. The World Soul is eternally creative and ordering because this constitutes its essential nature. No being acts other than according to its nature. Thus causation flows naturally from the nature of things and requires no external explanation or justification.

The causal hierarchy in Neoplatonism is absolute, yet paradoxically, it permits no actual separation or break. While the One is absolutely beyond all determination and all beings are determined, all beings receive their determination through their eternal dependence on and participation in the One. While the sensible world is farthest from the source and characterized by multiplicity, change, and privation, it is perpetually illuminated by the intelligible light that flows from above. Evil and privation exist precisely as the absence or diminishment of form and being as one descends the hierarchy, yet even in the material world, the traces of divine beauty and order remain visible.

The historical development of the Neoplatonic doctrine of causation shows increasing elaboration and systematization. Plotinus developed the basic doctrine of emanation and its causal implications. Porphyry systematized the doctrine, clarifying the relationship between cause and effect at each level and emphasizing the continuity of the causal chain. Iamblichus, while maintaining the basic emanationist framework, introduced intermediate realities and emphasized the role of divine intermediaries in the causal process. Later Neoplatonists, particularly Proclus, developed extraordinarily complex and detailed accounts of causation, introducing additional hypostases and intermediate levels to account for the full richness and order of reality while maintaining the fundamental principle of emanation.

The transmission of Neoplatonic causation to subsequent philosophical and theological traditions proved profoundly influential. Christian theology, particularly through the influence of Pseudo-Dionysius and medieval theology, adopted Neoplatonic emanationism, though often reinterpreting it within a creative framework. The tension between causation as creative production (in Christian thought) and causation as eternal emanation (in Neoplatonism) became a major point of philosophical development in medieval theology. Islamic philosophy, particularly Neoplatonically influenced schools, developed sophisticated accounts of causation derived from Plotinus. Renaissance Neoplatonists recovered the doctrine of emanation as central to their understanding of divine causation and cosmic order. Modern philosophy inherited and transformed these discussions of causation, though often without the metaphysical frameworks that gave them their original meaning and power.

The doctrine of causation illuminates several profound aspects of Neoplatonic metaphysics. First, it provides a comprehensive account of how all reality depends upon the One while the One remains absolutely transcendent and utterly simple. Second, it explains how multiplicity, change, and determination emerge from the utterly transcendent, undetermined One without requiring the One to become involved in change or determination. Third, it grounds the unity and continuity of the cosmos: all beings share in a common source and remain perpetually connected through an unbroken chain of causal dependence. Fourth, it validates the sensible world despite its ontological inferiority: it is genuinely real and good insofar as it participates in and is caused by intelligible realities.

In contemporary philosophy, Neoplatonic causation challenges mechanistic and materialist understandings of causation, which treat causes as efficient forces acting on passive matter. It suggests instead that causation is fundamentally a matter of dependence and participation, that lower realities are perpetually sustained in being by their participation in higher realities, that the universe is characterized by intrinsic order and hierarchy rather than random interaction. It proposes that understanding how things work requires understanding what they depend on and what they participate in, not merely analyzing efficient forces and material interactions.

For those who engage authentically with Neoplatonic philosophy, the doctrine of causation provides both intellectual coherence and spiritual meaning. It explains how the infinite divine source gives rise to the manifest universe without being diminished or involving the divine in creation. It grounds the accessibility of the divine to human consciousness: if all beings participate in and depend upon higher realities, and the infinite chain reaches to the divine source, then the divine is immanent in all things and available to those whose consciousness can attune to it. Causation, in this framework, is not merely a theoretical doctrine but a description of the soul's own situation and its potential for ascent toward its source.

sections.opening_definition: Causation is the principle of eternal emanation through which higher realities give rise to and sustain lower realities; a simultaneous and eternal relationship of creative dependence and overflow in which being, goodness, and form flow continuously from higher to lower levels of the cosmic hierarchy.
sections.historical_usage: The Greek term aition denoted cause and causal explanation. Classical philosophy developed various accounts of causation. Plotinus introduced the doctrine of emanation as the primary mode of causation, distinguishing Neoplatonic causation from efficient causation and material generation. Subsequent Neoplatonists elaborated and systematized this doctrine as the fundamental principle of cosmic order.
sections.philosophical_significance: Causation explains how the infinite, simple, transcendent One gives rise to multiplicity and determination without change. It demonstrates how all reality perpetually depends on and participates in what is higher. It grounds the unity and continuity of the cosmos despite its hierarchical stratification. It validates the reality and goodness of the sensible world as genuine expressions of intelligible reality.
sections.development_across_schools: Plotinus developed the doctrine of emanation as the fundamental mode of causation. Porphyry systematized the doctrine and its implications at each cosmic level. Iamblichus introduced intermediate realities while maintaining emanationism. Proclus developed the most elaborate and detailed accounts of causation with multiple hypostases and degrees of manifestation.
sections.transmission: Christian theology adopted Neoplatonic emanationism while reinterpreting it within a creative framework, creating productive tensions. Islamic philosophy developed Neoplatonic causation in the context of Islamic theology. Medieval Christian theology grappled with how Neoplatonic emanation relates to creation and divine causation. Renaissance Neoplatonists recovered the doctrine as central to metaphysics.
